ai: Retrieval runs as a multi-stage pipeline (src/ranking/pipeline.py). BM25 retrieves a candidate pool of 100 documents. Three further signals rescore that pool: lexical heuristics, dense embedding similarity, and link-graph authority. Combining them produces the top 10. Because BM25 is the only stage that retrieves anything and every later stage merely re-ranks, an unavailable external service costs the pipeline one signal rather than the whole query.
human: We retrieve documents based on a multi-stage pipeline. First, BM25 retrieves a pool of 50 candidate documents. Then, these documents are reranked using a weighted average of three other signals: 1) lexical heuristics, 2) semantic similarity with embeddings, and 3) link authority, before being returned.

ai: The journey to a gem-quality crystal begins by creating a supersaturated solution, where heat controls the solubility of the salt. You will start by heating approximately 200 mL of distilled water to near-boiling, around 80°C. Gradually stir in the copper sulfate powder—usually around 80 to 100 grams—until no more can dissolve and a few granules begin settling at the bottom. At this stage, the liquid will turn a deep, dark electric blue. Once fully dissolved, pour the hot solution through a coffee filter into a clean glass jar. Filtering removes undissolved specks and dust particles that would otherwise cause unwanted, irregular micro-crystals to form around the container instead of a single smooth crystal.
human: To grow a high quality copper sulfate crystal, first you need to create a supersaturated solution. Start by heating 200 mL of distilled water to near-boiling. Then, add 80 grams of copper sulfate powder to the water and keep stirring to make it dissolve faster. At this point, the solution should be a dark blue. Once all the powder has dissolved, pour it through a coffee filter into a clean glass jar. Filtering removes tiny undissolved particles and dust that would otherwise interfere with the crystal growth.

ai:
Two different costs, and only one of them is real.

Implementation: small. The recommended version is roughly 25–35 lines across three files — a new resyncTo on FishSwimPresentation (six scalar assignments), a resetTo on FishSurfaceController that's an extraction of two lines already running in the constructor rather than new logic, and a two-line call site on the false→true edge in SchoolingFish.setVisible. The four-line facing-only variant is smaller still and touches one file. Low risk either way: nothing changes for a fish that stays visible, so the steady-state render path is untouched.

Runtime, the resync itself: negligible. It fires once per invisible→visible transition per fish, not per frame, and the expensive part — setInitialSegments rebuilding the drag chain — costs about what one frame of that fish's normal spine solve costs. So each appearance pays roughly one extra frame of its own work, once. Even with a few dozen transitions per second across 300 fish, that's noise.

Runtime, the margin bump: this is the part that actually costs anything. Raising viewportCulling.marginUnits from 1 to ~4 widens the band of fish that get a full-rate render every frame. The cost scales with the added band area around the viewport, not with the margin directly — so it's a percentage of your current visible-fish count, and it's paid every frame forever, unlike the resync. Whether that's 5% or 25% more rendered fish depends on your viewport dimensions in world units, which I'd want measured rather than guessed.
human:
There are 2 different costs: code-wise, and performance-wise.

Code-wise, it's small. The recommended version is roughly 25-35 lines across three files.

Performance-wise, the margin bump is the one worth looking at. Raising viewportCulling.marginUnits from 1 to ~4 increases the number of fish that are rendered at full rate every frame. The exact amount depends on the banded area around your viewport in world units. I would measure this rather than guess. Meanwhile, the resync itself is negligible. It fires once per invisible -> visible transition per fish. Even with a few dozen transitions per second across 300 fish, that's noise.

ai: Brave New World, written by Aldous Huxley in 1932, was shaped by the historical and social conditions of the early twentieth century. One of the most significant historical influences was the Great Depression, which began in 1929 and created widespread fears about unemployment, poverty, and social instability. This economic crisis sparked debates about the role of government control and how society should be organized to prevent future crises. At the same time, advances in biology and medicine led to discussions about eugenics, birth control, and the possibility of improving society through the scientific management of reproduction. These ideas influenced public debates about population control, human development, and the extent to which the state should regulate private life. Rapid industrialization also had a major impact, particularly through Henry Ford's system of mass production, known as Fordism. While these methods emphasized efficiency and standardization, they also raised concerns about mechanization, conformity, and the loss of human individuality.
human: The novel Brave New World by Aldous Huxley was written based on historical and social conditions of the early twentieth century. Its most prominent influence was the Great Depression, which caused widespread fears about unemployment, poverty, and social instability. This economic crisis was the main cause of debates about how society should be organized, and the responsibility of the government in preventing crises like this from happening in the future. Meanwhile, improvements in the sciences like medicine and biotechnology sparked further discussions about eugenics, birth control and the question of whether it's humane to improve society through genetically modifying humans. Not only that, mass industrialization during this era also played a part, especially through the system of mass production introduced by Henry Ford. Although these methods improved efficiency and standardized the manufacturing procedures of the time, they nonetheless caused people to worry about losing their individuality.
